market_context: United States; household garlic storage and use.
title: Can You Eat Sprouted Garlic?

seo.title: Can You Eat Sprouted Garlic?
seo.meta_description: Yes. A garlic clove with a green sprout is still edible if it is firm and free of mold or rot. Remove the sprout if its flavor is too bitter.
seo.search_intent: Decide whether garlic with a green sprout is safe to eat and when it should be discarded.

excerpt: Yes. Sprouting is a sign of age and renewed plant growth, not toxicity. A firm, dry clove without mold or rot is still usable; the green center can taste sharper or more bitter and may be removed for flavor.
content_html:
You split open a garlic clove and find a green shoot running through the center. That shoot does not make the garlic poisonous. It means the clove has come out of dormancy and is trying to grow.

University of California food-preservation guidance notes that garlic stored too long may shrivel or begin to sprout and that neither condition is harmful by itself. Oregon State University Extension likewise states that sprouted garlic is still edible.

The biggest change is flavor

The center sprout can taste more grassy, sharp, or bitter than the rest of the clove, especially once it is long and bright green. If you are making a raw dressing, aioli, pesto, or another preparation where garlic flavor is exposed, slice the clove lengthwise and remove the sprout if you want a cleaner taste.

For soups, braises, and cooked sauces, a small sprout often makes little practical difference.

Sprouted is not the same as spoiled

Judge the whole clove. Usable garlic should still be reasonably firm and smell like garlic. A soft, watery, slimy clove with mold, wet brown decay, or an unpleasant fermented odor has a spoilage problem that is separate from sprouting.

Why garlic sprouts in storage

Time, temperature, and moisture all matter. UC ANR recommends storing dry garlic in a cool, dry, dark, well-ventilated place. A typical refrigerator near 40°F (4°C) is not ideal for long-term storage of dry bulbs and can stimulate sprouting after cold exposure.

A ventilated pantry location is usually better than a sealed plastic bag beside a stove.

Can you eat the sprout itself?

Yes. Young garlic greens and scapes are also used as food. Whether you leave the center sprout in is primarily a flavor decision.

Practical rule: green sprout plus a firm, clean clove is fine; mold, slime, wet rot, or an off odor is a reason to discard it.

faq.question: Is the green center of garlic toxic?
faq.answer: No. It is a growing shoot. It may taste more bitter, but it does not make the clove toxic.

faq.question: Do I always need to remove the sprout?
faq.answer: No. Removing it is mainly about flavor, especially in raw or delicate dishes.

faq.question: When should sprouted garlic be thrown away?
faq.answer: Discard it when it also has mold, wet rot, slime, extensive softening, or a clearly unpleasant odor.
